w: Croatia's oldest museum, founded in 1820, holds some 150,000 pieces from ancient Salona - Roman glass, clay lamps, gems and coins - plus a courtyard lapidarium of stone inscriptions. The collection runs from Greek colonization of the Adriatic through Roman rule to the early Croatian state.
_facts: Oldest museum in Croatia, established 1820 by decree of the Dalmatian government in Zadar
Around 150,000 artifacts: Salona stone inscriptions, Greco-Hellenistic ceramics, Roman glass, clay lamps, coins
Two-story main building with arcades housing a lapidarium and garden

s: A modern cathedral built on a borrowed stone
w: Consecrated in 1980, barely older than most of its congregation, this co-cathedral carries deeper roots than its date suggests: its first stone was carried over from the old Croatian church of St Peter in nearby Salona. Rome elevated it to co-cathedral status in 1987.
_facts: Construction began December 1979 with the blessing of the first stone, brought from the old Croatian church of St Peter's in Salona
Completed 1980; elevated to co-cathedral of the Archdiocese of Split-Makarska by the Holy See on 11 May 1987
Officially dedicated 27 July 1987

s: The only museum built for Croatia's medieval story
w: The only Croatian museum devoted purely to the early medieval Croats, this collection has moved house four times - Knin, Sinj, Klis and finally a purpose-built home in Split in 1976. Jewellery, weapons and clay figurines fill the halls, alongside Europe's largest set of Old Croatian Latin stone inscriptions.
_facts: Only museum in Croatia dedicated to Croats' medieval cultural artifacts, 7th-15th centuries
Founded in Knin 1893, moved to Sinj, then Klis, finally Split in a purpose-built complex opened 1976
Holdings include jewellery, weapons, wicker and clay figurines; largest collection of Old Croatian Latin epigraphic monuments in Europe

s: The emperor's front door, sealed shut for centuries
w: Diocletian's main gate into his retirement palace was built to impress, the grandest of the old town's four Roman gates. Medieval Split walled it up, stripping its columns and statues. Modern restoration reopened it, and visitors now walk through the same threshold the emperor once used.
_facts: The Northern Gate, one of four principal Roman gates into Diocletian's Palace / stari grad
Built as the palace's main gate, elaborately decorated to mark its status
Sealed off in the Middle Ages, losing its columns and statuary; reopened and repaired in modern times

s: Seven centuries of Dalmatian art in an old hospital
w: Founded in 1931, Split's fine art collection spans the 14th century to the present, with major Croatian names - Vlaho Bukovac and Ivan Mestrovic among them - hanging alongside an extensive icon collection. Since 2009 it has lived in a fully refurbished former hospital building, a fitting second life for old walls.
_facts: Founded 1931; permanent exhibition of paintings and sculptures from the 14th century to the present
Works by Vlaho Bukovac, Mato Celestin Medovic, Branislav Deskovic, Ivan Mestrovic, Emanuel Vidovic, Ignjat Job; extensive icon collection
Relocated in 2009 to a refurbished old hospital building in Split

s: A church squeezed into a Roman gatehouse
w: Barely bigger than a corridor, St Martin's was fitted into the old guardhouse of the Golden Gate itself, making it one of the oldest churches in Split. Its 11th-century chancel screen survives intact, tended today by the Dominican sisters next door. Step inside and you're standing inside Diocletian's own city wall.
_facts: Built into a small guardhouse space within the ancient Golden Gate of Diocletian's northern wall
One of the oldest churches in Split; known for its fine 11th-century chancel screen
In the care of the Dominican sisters, who have a monastery next door; open to public visits

s: A thousand-year-old six-leaf chapel, still in use
w: Among Dalmatia's early medieval churches, this small pre-Romanesque chapel stands out for its unusual six-leaf plan - arches strung around an irregular circle, unchanged since the 8th to 11th centuries. It ranks among Croatia's most protected heritage monuments, and Sunday Mass is still said here outside summer.
_facts: Pre-Romanesque Roman Catholic church, dated to the 8th-11th centuries
Unusual six-leaf structure of semicircular arches around an irregular circle
Registered as highest-category Croatian Cultural Heritage; active parish, Sunday Mass 8:30am except mid-June to September

s: Naval history stacked inside a 17th-century fortress
w: Ship models and naval relics fill a 19th-century building raised inside the older Gripe Fortress walls. The museum dates only to 1997, but its lineage runs back through a Yugoslav Navy institution to a 1925 original, absorbing older collections along the way.
_facts: Housed in a 19th-century building built within the 17th-century Gripe Fortress
Established 1997 as successor to a 1925 Maritime Museum, then a Yugoslav Navy Military-Maritime Museum from 1960
Also inherited the collection of the Maritime Museum of the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts (1956-1985)

s: The gate that still faces Rome's old road east
w: The Eastern Gate of Diocletian's Palace once looked straight toward Epetia, the Roman settlement now known as Stobrec. Plainer than the Golden Gate but no less ancient, the Silver Gate has funneled traffic in and out of Split's old town for some seventeen centuries, still doing exactly the job it was built for.
_facts: One of the four principal Roman gates into the stari grad, part of Diocletian's Palace
The Eastern Gate, facing toward the Roman town of Epetia (today Stobrec)

s: A sculptor's own house, built to hold his life's work
w: Croatia's great 20th-century sculptor designed this gallery and its grounds himself, so building and art were made for each other. Plaster models sit beside finished bronze, marble and wood pieces. Nearby, the restored Kastelet-Crikvine chapel holds wooden wall panels he carved by hand.
_facts: Art museum dedicated to 20th-century sculptor Ivan Mestrovic, built on his own plans
Holdings include plaster models, and finished works in bronze, marble and wood
Nearby Kastelet-Crikvine, a restored chapel, houses wooden wall panels carved by Mestrovic

s: A cemetery erased for reasons nobody explained
w: A Benedictine monastery once stood on this small peninsula; centuries later, one of Croatia's most admired cemeteries replaced it. In the 20th century, Communist authorities tore the graveyard out entirely - the reason was never recorded. What's left is a quiet forest park over history nobody explains.
_facts: Small peninsula in southwestern Split; site of a Benedictine monastery and church in the Middle Ages
One of Croatia's most beautiful 19th-century cemeteries was built here
Cemetery removed in the 20th century by Communist authorities; reason never established. Now a forest park
